blocks.text: In 1901 Max Planck suggested that energy is radiated or absorbed in discrete packets called quanta (singular quantum), rather than as a continuous wave. Each quantum belongs to radiation of a single frequency, and its energy E is proportional to its frequency f: E = hf (18.1), where h is Planck's constant, 6.63 x 10^-34 J s. Planck received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1918 for his discovery of energy quanta.

blocks.title: For your information
blocks.text: Planck's constant h is a fundamental constant of quantum theory; another important constant, the speed of light c, is a constant of the special theory of relativity.

Planck suggested that, just as matter is made of a large number of tiny particles, radiation energy from a hot source is granular, and he assumed this was due to some property of the atoms producing it. Einstein extended the idea: packets of energy are an integral part of all electromagnetic radiation and cannot be subdivided. He called these indivisible bundles of energy photons. A beam of light of wavelength lambda is a stream of photons travelling at speed c, each carrying energy E = hf.

From the theory of relativity, E = mc^2, and the momentum of a photon is p = mc, so E = pc (18.2). Then pc = hf, so p = hf/c, and since c = f lambda, the momentum of a photon is p = h/lambda (18.3). Because a photon carries momentum, light can exert a force (radiation pressure) on a surface it strikes.

Quantum theory can be extended to any system, such as a mass oscillating on a spring, but there the energy steps are far too small to detect, so any particle nature is invisible. Quantum effects matter only for atom-sized objects, where h is significant in any detectable change of energy.
